speechtext:
It was proclaimed just four days before the provincial election. There is no doubt that a national health scheme for Canada can only be put into effect, and be effective, when there is basic education with regard to health and welfare services in this country. But surely if the figures given by the hon. member for Regina City of the basic investigations that have been carried out over the years are true, then we have reached the time when we can take another step forward in these health services which are so necessary to our Canadian people.
I am sure that Canadians were startled during the last war -when it was proven that out of the men enlisting for active service approximately 42 per cent were unfit. That condition is not much better today. In fact it is worse, if the figures given recently by Lieutenant Colonel Matthews are correct, in which he states that 50 per cent enlisting today are physically and emotionally unfit for service in our armed forces. Surely it is time we made another step forward. We in the C.C.F. believe that national health insurance is the next forward step that should be made in Canada toward an over-all social security program for our people.
There are three distinct differences of opinion with regard to this matter. The Liberals state their position quite clearly in the speech from the throne. They say this:
Much has been accomplished since the inauguration in 1948 of the five-year national health grants program to strengthen and improve, in co-operation with the provincial governments, the health and hospital facilities available to our people. To ensure the continued expansion of this important work, my government proposes to ask you to give consideration to the extension, with certain changes, of this program of co-operation with the provincial governments.
I do not know what the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) may announce as to what that further step will be; whether it is just going to be an extension


of the present hospital grants; whether it is going to mean an increase in those hospital grants, or whether it is going to mean what I believe, and what we in this group believe, should be a new step forward, which will give to our people complete health care. I say that because I am convinced we have reached the point in Canada where we can take this step, by extending the services we now have and which we are able to extend.
The health survey tabled by the government in Saskatchewan indicates that in that province we have carried on an experiment in provincial health services which could serve as a guide to other provinces, and to the dominion, in extending our medical services to full coverage at this time.
As the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. McCusker) said, medical health services in western Canada have been growing over a period of years. The municipal doctor plan was inaugurated after the first war, and there are now in Saskatchewan 110 physicians with municipal doctor contracts. These physicians provide a varying range of services to approximately 200,000 persons in 107 municipalities in which there are municipal doctors.
Not only this, but in that province a great number of our physicians are engaged in some form of social medicine. Out of 563 active practitioners, 58 are employed in hospitals or institutions, 110 have municipal doctor contracts, and 36 are engaged in the Swift Current health area. This means that in Saskatchewan 204 out of 563 medical practitioners are already engaged in some form of social medicine. So with the introduction of a federal scheme we would simply be extending something already in existence in that province. I think members of the medical profession agree that some form of medical health insurance is necessary. As a matter of fact, already our doctors are engaging voluntarily in the clinic form of medicine. In Saskatchewan the trend among the members of the medical profession is to practise in partnerships and groups. The figures show that 205, or 43 per cent of the 479 general practitioners and specialists are engaged in this type of practice.
An examination of the distribution according to age groups reveals that in age groups below 40 physicians practising in groups or partnerships outnumber those practising alone by a ratio of four to three. The converse is true of age groups from 40 to 49 years and from 50 to 59 years. Of the 86 general practitioners and specialists over 60, 65 are practising alone.
In other words today the doctors themselves are voluntarily forming clinics to work

at their profession. The day of the individual practitioner is over in Canada; and by instituting some over-all form of health insurance we will only be continuing something that is already growing in Canada.
The attitude of the Progressive Conservative party in this matter is expressed quite clearly in its amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Paragraph (d) of that amendment offered by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) says this:
(d) To conduct inquiries in consultation with the provincial governments, so that necessary information may be available for the dominion and provincial governments to consider jointly a national health insurance program.
Well, evidence was placed before the house by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) indicating that there have been some 30 general surveys and reports in the last ten years. Today the hon. member for Regina City tabled the reports of five provinces and their surveys with respect to health insurance. Surely we do not need another one at this time. Surely we have reached the point where, over the years, we have built up a sense of the need for some further medical health care, to the point where we are prepared to take the necessary steps forward at this time.
That is why we in the C.C.F. offered our amendment to the amendment. Moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), it stated that we should recommend legislation at this session establishing a nation-wide health insurance program, with provision for provincial administration. I believe that is the position taken by the great majority of people in this country. The government has received the annual reports of the various labour organizations, including the A.F. of L., the C.I.O. and the Catholic Confederation of Labour. In nearly all these annual reports the recommendation is made that an over-all medical health scheme for Canada be instituted.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture, women's institutes and farm unions-practically every organization in Canada, in making its report to our government, has asked for health insurance. A Gallup poll indicated that 75 per cent of our people are in favour of a national health insurance program. Surely this should be an indication to the government as to the position taken by people across this country.
In the C.C.F. all we are doing is trying to voice the will of the people in respect of a federal health service. I am sure if the Liberal party is to meet the needs of the people it must do more at this session than simply take another step, or extend steps
The Address-Mr. Wright already taken. It is true that health grants to the provinces have assisted. It is also true that the hospital grants now given are not sufficient. As a matter of fact the $1,000 per bed given by the dominion government, and supplemented in an equal amount by the various provincial governments, represents today only the increased cost of building hospitals in Canada since the time the grant was first given in 1948. There has been a tremendous increase in costs, and the grants only meet that increase; in fact, I do not think they do meet the whole of it. Municipalities are still burdened with the major cost of hospital construction.
I think that in the matter of hospital construction the municipalities must accept a share of the responsibility. In my view the building and the administration of hospitals throughout the country should remain under municipal control, because the closer one gets to the people in the administration of local services the more economically they are likely to be operated.
That has been the object of the health scheme in Saskatchewan. The province has tried to assist the municipalities in building these facilities. The moment some of these services are made available to the people you create the desire or the will to build the facilities to meet those services. It was the general hospitalization scheme introduced in Saskatchewan that caused the municipalities to begin a hospital building program. When the people in the province found that these services were to be made available to them, immediately they put pressure on their municipal governments to create the facilities, so they might use the hospitalization scheme then introduced.
The same thing would take place right across Canada. If we passed a national health scheme for the Dominion of Canada we would find a desire created, even in those provinces which may today be below the average in hospital beds available to their population, that would force municipalities to build the necessary facilities to make the act effective. That is why we in the C.C.F. believe we should make a real step forward in health insurance at this session of parliament.
I should now like to refer to another matter which is included in the speech from the throne. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) are now in Great Britain at the commonwealth conference on trade relations. We do not know what the outcome of that conference may be. We do not know what recommendations may come out of it. One press report states that the matter of the revaluation of gold is under consideration and that the

The Address-Mr. Wright question of exchange rates may be taken up. I am sure every member of the house is anxious that out of this conference shall come better trade relations not only within the commonwealth but throughout the free areas of the world. It seems to me if that is to be accomplished there are certain basic things which we must take into consideration.
We in Canada and on the North American continent are in a very fortunate position. During the last war Canada was able to build up many of its productive facilities. We were able to increase the plant capacity of the country for manufacturing. We were able to increase our production of various raw materials. After the war we found ourselves in a much better position as far as trade was concerned than before the war started. Just the opposite was the case in Europe and in Great Britain. On the continent particularly they found that many of their factories had been destroyed. In England some of their factories were destroyed, and others became obsolete through almost continuous use in the production of war materials.
Let us see how we increased the value of our plant capacity in Canada. I am going to use the Aluminum Company of Canada as an example. During the war the capital of that company expanded by over $100 million. That plant was paid for out of the price which we obtained for aluminum. One of the greatest buyers of aluminum was Great Britain. In other words Great Britain, through her purchases of aluminum in Canada, made a very large investment in the expansion of that plant and the production of aluminum in this country, while at the same time much of her plant and equipment was becoming obsolete.
That can be carried into practically every field of manufacture. Our allies during the war, through the price they paid Canada for much of the equipment and material they needed, and which they used in bringing of the war to a successful conclusion, brought about the expansion of our plant and equipment. We find now when the war is over that we have expanded our plant and equipment in Canada while the markets for much of the goods supplied at one time by Great Britain have been lost to her. Her investments in this country were dissipated during the war or were used at that time for the purchase of raw materials and goods from this country. Now we are finding that we cannot trade with Great Britain, we cannot sell our farm products to Great Britain.
You know, it seems there is something wrong when we in this country have an abundance of feed grain and all the facilities


to produce bacon in large quantities, yet in Great Britain the people are on a ration of two or three ounces of bacon a week. Are we genuine in our relationships with our NATO partners when we say to some of the European countries and Great Britain, for instance, as some people in this country do- I am very glad to say there are not many members of parliament in this class-that they should reduce their standard of living even further? These people say that Great Britain should do this so she may take her place alongside us in the production of the necessary materials to secure our protection and theirs against aggression in the world.
It seems to me that we have to reciprocate. We have to do something which Great Britain did in the early years of Canada's development. In those years Great Britain invested a lot of money in Canada in our railroads, in our early manufacturing plants and other enterprises that brought about the development of the country. Surely now in the hour of Great Britain's need, after she has dissipated her resources in two great wars, we should be prepared to reciprocate and try to build up in Great Britain and other NATO countries some of the plant and equipment which they used lavishly for our protection during the last war.
How can we do that? I think the proposals made by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar should be given serious consideration. If we want to sell our agricultural products to Great Britain there is only one way in which Great Britain can pay for them, and that is in goods or services. She cannot produce these goods and services with her present plant and equipment. Therefore it seems to me that the wise thing for us to do would be to accept sterling for some of the goods and services we can supply to her. Let us sell her bacon, sell her apples, sell her cheese, accept sterling and invest that sterling in plant and equipment in Great Britain to assist in improving her ability to produce more goods and services so that later she can pay us for the products we produce in Canada.
I do not think that we can solve our trade problems by manipulating the price of gold or manipulating exchanges. The price of gold and the manipulation of exchanges simply are a barometer indicating what has taken place in trade. It may be a balance wheel to a certain extent, but the only true balance wheel in trade is the trading of goods for goods; and until the countries with which we are dealing are able to produce the goods we need at a price at which we are prepared to accept them, then trade will be a one-way street and will die. I agree with

much of what the hon. member for Charlotte <Mr. Stuart) said the other day. We have to take down some of the barriers this country has erected against trade. We have to try to make trade a two-way street. We have to invest in some of these countries with which we want to trade so they can produce goods and services to pay for the things we have to sell to them. It does not make sense to see an agricultural policy being followed in this country which would restrict our production of agricultural products to what we can consume in this country when there are other countries engaged with us in a common defence program under NATO that have a standard of living which is much below ours.
This matter of exchange is rather a mystery to a lot of people. It seems an anomaly that today, through the manipulation of our exchange-I do not like the use of the word "manipulation", but through the fluctuations of our exchange-we, as western wheat producers, should be receiving about 20 cents a bushel, I believe-and it was 25 or 26 cents a bushel some three or four weeks ago-less than we were receiving six months ago when our Canadian dollar was 10 cents under the United States dollar. Under the international wheat agreement the last quotation I saw was $1.76. That price was $1.98 some six months ago. It has been as low as $1.72.
We are receiving less, yet the British are paying more for that grain than they were paying previously, just because the price paid by the British was fixed on the basis of the United States dollar. Usually when the producer receives less for a product one naturally assumes the consumer is paying less for it. That is the whole basis for fluctuations in price. When the producer receives less the consumer pays less, and because of the lesser price he is paying he consumes a bit more and you get an adjustment in price; but that is not what is taking place today. We are getting less and the British are paying the same for their purchases of our wheat. Not only that, the millers in Canada are paying less for the wheat because of the increase in the value of our Canadian dollar. They purchase the wheat at the international wheat agreement price. Some six months ago they were paying $1.98 plus regular carrying and diversion charges. Today they are paying the international wheat agreement price of $1.76; but are consumers in this country getting flour any cheaper as a result of that? Not at all. The price of flour has remained the same even though the price of wheat to millers has dropped by as much as 25 cents
The Address-Mr. Wright a bushel. Somebody must be making a greater profit out of the milling of wheat than they were before.
Notwithstanding all this the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) indicated to this house, and to the committee on agriculture, that he was pretty adamant in his position on wheat, that the domestic price for wheat should be the same as the international wheat agreement price. Surely he cannot argue today, with the millers buying the wheat at from 20 to 25 cents less because of the fluctuations in the exchange rates, that it is a position that we in Canada should be in now. Surely there is no reason, just because there was a rise in the value of the Canadian dollar, for the millers of this country to be able to purchase wheat cheaper by 20 to 26 cents. If they do, then certainly that cheaper wheat should be reflected in cheaper flour to the consumers of this country, and that has not been the case to date.
The primary producers of this country are taking a tremendous loss today because of the fluctuations in the exchange rates. Estimates have been made by various authorities. I have here an editorial in the Western Producer which indicates that the loss this year to the western grain producers may amount to as much as $150 million. That is a serious loss. They state here:
It is possible that Mr. Abbott is not fully cognizant of the enormous penalty paid by prairie wheat growers as a result of the exchange situation. It is costing them a full 25 cents per bushel when compared with the rate prevailing at the time the wheat agreement was negotiated. That will amount to something like $150 million on the grain going to market this year. It will cost a farmer $250 on every 1,000 bushels of wheat. The farmer who harvests 10.000 bushels of wheat is nicked to the tune of $2,500.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) may think that is all right, that the western wheat producers should have $150 million less to spend on goods and services this year, but there will not be the same demand for those goods and services. They will not buy as many refrigerators or as much new machinery as they might have had they received this additional purchasing power. It enables the government to keep down the cost of living in this country, but surely the primary producers-and the pulp and paper and lumber people are in the same position as the western farmers-should not be asked to subsidize the lowering of the cost of living in this country. That is what is taking place with the present exchange fluctuations.
It is all very well to say that it is fine for our Canadian dollar to be at a premium over the United States dollar, but some

The Address-Mr. Wright people are paying a pretty high price for that fact, and they are the primary producers, the wheat producers in western Canada.
We all agree that we should have an international wheat agreement. I think 95 per cent of the wheat producers in western Canada are behind the wheat board and the government in trying to negotiate another wheat agreement. What we do object to in western Canada is that when we have negotiated these long-term agreements the government should then change the conditions under which we as producers have to fulfil them. That has happened twice now. When we entered into the British contract in 1947 there was a price ceiling on most of the things which went into the cost of production in this country. Immediately after we made that agreement the government took off the price ceilings in this country with the result that the producers, whose product had been sold at a fixed price for three years and at a negotiated price in the last year, saw their cost of production go up by from 25 to 50 per cent. As a result that agreement, which had been a good agreement as far as the wheat producers were concerned when it was entered- into, became not nearly so good, because conditions over which the government had control changed. Now the same thing is taking place with regard to the international wheat agreement.
When we entered into the international wheat agreement the price was fixed on the basis of the United States dollar, and during much of that contract as a result of the price being fixed on the basis of the United States dollar, we were getting for our wheat $1.98 plus carrying charges. The government then, on the advice of the Conservative party, did away with the foreign exchange control board and freed the Canadian dollar. Immediately that dollar began to rise until it reached $1.04J as compared with the United States dollar. That resulted at once in a change in the conditions under which wheat growers were producing their product to fulfil the agreement entered into on their behalf. As I said before it meant that they would get 20 to 25 cents a bushel less for their grain, because this government changed the conditions that Canada had control over, thereby reducing the price received by the producers for their product.
That is the surest way by which we can discourage our people or attempt to discourage our people from entering into these agreements. In western Canada we certainly believe in these long-term agreements and

we believe that the government, in negotiating them, should take the advice of some of the officials of our various organizations in western Canada. I have in my hand a copy of an address given by J. H. Wesson at the annual meeting of the Saskatchewan wheat pool. I believe that in a couple of sentences he sums up the position of the producers of western Canada very effectively. He states:
I think we should concern ourselves with this one point, and I hope you raise this in the country, What are we likely to get in prices if we don't have an agreement? That should be our concern.
He continues later:
In other words the whole principle of international agreement, that we debated over 22 years ago, was that we wanted prices fair to the producer and fair to the consumer alike, and we wanted to get away from this so-called three-dollar wheat and the next year 40-cent wheat. So I want to repeat we can't expect to get peak prices under an international wheat agreement, but we don't face those cellar prices of 38 and 40 cents as we did in the black thirties. I think the most important thing that our people should consider today is not how much we could get in a ceiling price, as how high we can get the floor price for our own protection for the future of the next four years.
I think that sums up pretty well the attitude of the western wheat producer. I hope that in negotiating another wheat contract our government will take this into consideration.
For just a few minutes I want to deal with the question of transportation facilities. We are going to have quite a problem in getting our crop to market this year. I feel that the wheat board and the transportation companies did a reasonably good job in moving our crop last year. In western Canada we have had two years in which our crop was out of condition, in which a large percentage of it was in the lower grades and a large percentage was tough and damp. These crops have been moved to market without any serious loss. I believe the wheat board and the various authorities who have had charge of the movement of those crops have done a reasonable job. It is true that there have been certain localities in which conditions have existed which should not have existed. Some localities were able to get their crop to market quicker than other areas. But taken as a whole there has been a reasonable attempt made to move our crop to market in an orderly manner.
This year we are going to face problems as great or greater. It is going to take all the facilities we have available to market our crop before the next crop year. One of our facilities which I believe should be extended at this time is the port of Churchill. We have there a government elevator which has approximately a 2 [DOT] 5 million bushel capacity.

This year we have moved through that port the largest amount of grain that has been moved to date, about 8J million bushels. Anyone who knows anything about the movement of grain knows the problem there is when you move 8J million bushels of grain during the short period that port is open, and with an elevator capacity of approximately 2 [DOT] 5 million bushels. In other words there is about 2 million bushels capacity available there, and the space for the other half million bushels has to be used for working space.
If we are to increase the deliveries through that port, as I believe we should, then action should be taken. By delivering grain through that port we can deliver a much greater amount with the same number of box cars than we could if those box cars were used to bring grain to Port Arthur and Fort William, and the amount would be even greater if those box cars must be used to bring grain to eastern Canada. The On-to-the-Bay Association in western Canada is an active body. They have made certain recommendations to the government upon which I believe the government should take action.
They suggest first that the elevator capacity at Churchill should be doubled before the opening of the 1953 season. In answer to a question the other day the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) indicated that this matter would be given consideration. I hope that consideration is going to be given in sufficient time to enable us to handle more of our grain through that port in the 1953 season.
The second recommendation reads:
In view of increase in overseas and coastal trade, enlargement of dock and equipment to allow berthing and loading two more ships, making berth space for five beats.
3.	Essential that an effective ice patrol by air be organized out of Churchill by plane or helicopter effective mid July until late August with assurance that all information and advice be given ships before they approach and leave Churchill.
4.	All season effective air patrol of the straits.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I at the outset offer my sincere congratulations to the mover (Mr. Deslieres) and the seconder (Mr. Schneider) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, for the able way in which they fulfilled the task entrusted to them. Their speeches show without the shadow of a doubt that the electors of Brome-Missisquoi and of Waterloo North have every reason to be proud of the members they recently chose to represent them.
Before beginning my remarks, I would like to mention some incidents that occurred during the past year about which the people of Lake St. John have reason to be proud.
First, last February, their member had the honour of being chosen as seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I then had the pleasure of telling the house of the beauty, the wealth and the prodigious development of that part of our country.
Later, in June to be exact, with the encouragement and co-operation of my colleagues from Charlevoix (Mr. Maltais) and from Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Boisvert), I was able to demonstrate on the spot to a group of 65 members and their wives how well-founded were the statements I had made in my speech on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. This trip, I am sure, was much appreciated and has been for quite a few a true revelation. The sentiment of pride, felt by the people of my constituency and the people of the whole Saguenay district, was unsurpassed except for the honour and the pleasure they had in welcoming such a delegation of distinguished and keenly interested people.
Visits like these are surely enough to revive our pride in being Canadians and to strengthen our desire for national unity.
Finally, we had the honour, during the month of August, to welcome the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). He was able to appreciate for himself the immense indus-

312	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. A. Gauthier trial possibilities of a district newly opened but still full of promise. We are thankful to Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent for the interest he takes in every part of our immense country; the prosperity enjoyed in this "kingdom" of the Saguenay is not peculiar to this part of Canada, for it spreads all over the country.
Mr. Speaker, like every other member of this house and every other Canadian, I was proud and happy to learn of the elevation by our holy father the Pope of His Excellency Archbishop Leger to the exalted rank of cardinal. The people from the constituency of Lake St. John extend to him their most heartfelt congratulations, assure him of their filial submission and respectful good wishes.
Last week, in this house, we heard some severe criticism levelled at the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Breton), in an excellent speech delivered yesterday, supported the government's action in regard to television. He did so with skill, with convincing arguments. He deserves our congratulations.
I do not intend to deal with this matter in such an exhaustive way. Still I would like to express my own opinion. The Liberal party has always championed Canadian unity and, for the past 25 years, and especially under its present leader has attempted to bring into play all those factors favourable to the development of a true Canadian spirit and of an attitude worthy of a sovereign nation mindful of the duties which it is called upon to discharge.
Radio broadcasting goes back to 1919, but each station has been operated first and foremost for the income which such and such program could produce; unfortunately, there was no organized body capable of guiding radio activities in the interest of Canadian listeners and1 in that of Canada as a nation.
In 1929, the government which was then headed by the Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King, in a foresighted gesture, instituted a royal commission of inquiry presided over by Sir John Aird. Insisting on the fact that radio broadcasting was a responsible public institution and that it is an excellent means of popular education, that commission, even if it recognized the laudable efforts of private stations, made recommendations which were eventually to bring about a system which was to become one of the greatest factors of national unity and better understanding between the different racial groups of this country.

The opinion claiming that radio broadcasting should serve, first and foremost, to create and maintain a Canadian culture is now firmly established and does not give rise to any discussion. In order to allow for the implementation of such a policy, in order that its application may become a constant practice, it was necessary to have a directing body entrusted with the supervision of foreign broadcasts, with the fostering of programs liable to awaken national interest, in short, with the orientation of broadcasting to programs of Canadian inspiration, more in keeping with our national mentality.
I am not suggesting that it was necessary to give this body the name of C.B.C. or Canadian Broadcasting Corporation or any other name but I declare that even if it were to exist outside the national network, it would be necessary to grant the latter privileges and advantages which would allow it to attain the objective for which it was created.
What is true of radio is even more so of television. The present government cannot repeat the mistake committed in the early days of radio. I for one would not want to see a menace of cultural annexation by the Americans threaten once again the present generation. Has it not been said before the Massey commission on national development in arts, letters and sciences, by a representative of a private station that the best way to raise the cultural level in Canada would be to take full advantage of the culture which has progressed most rapidly, that of the United States.
Do you not believe, Mr. Speaker, that the conscious or unconscious tendency towards the acquisition of American culture greatly endangers the future of our young nation, such a tendency being moreover favoured by economic factors, inasmuch as private broadcasting stations are considered. From a strictly commercial point of view, it is easy to see that a private station owner would be strongly tempted to import films or to pipe in programs produced by American stations more cheaply than in Canada.
For that reason, I favour the present policy of the government in respect to television. It is advisable that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation be the first to guide television and produce programs of Canadian inspiration.
I do not pretend that the C.B.C. is a perfect institution: it has made errors and it will likely make others. Together with the members of the Massey-Levesque commission, I believe that some of the gaps can be filled in. As an example of that, I give the following conclusion put forward by the royal commission:

That persons engaged in radio broadcasting in Canada directly and adversely affected by a final decision of the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation on any matter in which this board has final authority be granted the right of appeal to a federal court against substantial miscarriage of justice.
Although there might be room for improvement as far as the status of the C.B.C. is concerned or for the amendment of some of its regulations, I cannot accept the conclusions of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Courte-manche) who says, at page 76 of Hansard:
Neither do I hesitate to accept the conclusions of Basil Dean, whose texts published in the Calgary Herald have been translated into French and published in pamphlet form under the title "Freedom of the Airwaves" In so far as television is concerned, his conclusions are as follows:	Television in Canada, he writes, will have to be submitted to some sort of control-of course-but not to that of the C.B.C. It should be the same kind of control that is asked for radio-a purely technical control. That control should be exercised by an independent commission, similar to the board of transport commissioners; that commission should assign the radio frequencies and television wave-lengths. That is, after all, the only formal control that should exist.
The hon. member says that he accepts the conclusions of Basil Dean; it means, in other words, that he would be favourable to a purely technical control the sole purpose of which would be to assign television wavelengths. It is truly impossible for me to support such policy.
Mr. Speaker, we from Quebec have particular reasons to resist the threat of American cultural assimilation. We have a profound devotion to our language, our religion and our traditions-in a word, to our French culture.
The present policy of this government is favourable to the growth of a distinctive Canadian culture, as well as to the maintenance of French culture, which is an absolutely essential element in the existence of this Canadian nation of ours.
Certainly, sooner or later, private enterprise will have a hand in television, but the latter will have, meanwhile, learned to serve the national interest. '
It will be pointed out to us that censorship may play a truly useful part in the cleaning up of television broadcasts. I agree. I might add in passing, too, that censorship belongs to the provincial field and must be applied by provincial governments. Still, by its very nature, censorship exerts a purely passive or negative action, in that it prevents the spread of what may be more particularly injurious to the morals and education of our youth. It can never replace with any efficiency a state-supported body whose mission is to foster and maintain the growth of Canadian unity, of a true Canadianism. In short, we must
The Address-Mr. Fair have a positive and constructive television policy. There is the whole difference, Mr. Speaker, between the policy put forward by the Progressive Conservative party and that expounded by the Liberal party.
The former favours a policy of abstention, a purely negative or passive one, whereas the latter demonstrates in this connection, as in others, foresight, realism and patriotism.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate this afternoon I feel that we are coming back to finish up some of the jobs we should have done last session, or perhaps two or three sessions ago. I refer now to the War Veterans Allowance Act.
It will be remembered that for some time we on the opposition side have tried to have something done about that, and the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) was good enough to set up a committee at the last session and make certain changes. Until that time a single veteran was getting an allowance of $40 a month and a married veteran $70 a month. Many of us who had been out around the country did not feel, and still do not feel that that is sufficient for those veterans. Recommendations were made that this be increased from $40 to $60 and from $70 to $120; but when, the bill was brought in provision was made to increase the allowance for the single veteran to $50 a month, and for the married veteran to $90 a month.
I have not heard any veterans' organization, or any veterans, say they are satisfied with that amount. We must remember that since 1939 the value of our dollar has dropped to 50 cents. I think everybody will agree that no veteran can exist on that allowance. Many of them are suffering from very poor health. In my opinion, instead of putting them off with $50 and $90 they should have preferred treatment, because they are the men who, some years ago, went overseas and offered everything they had, namely their lives, in order that Canada should be free. Had this not been done many of us would not be able to sit here in comfort in this house today and discuss this and many other matters.
On many occasions in the past I have referred to a statement made by Sir Robert Borden, who was at that time prime minister of Canada. I am going to bring the matter a little more up to date with another statement by the late prime minister, William Lyon Mackenzie King. This is taken from
314	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Fair Hansard of February 24, 1930, at page 44, and has to do with the veterans' problem. Mr. King had this to say:
May I say that after giving a great deal of time and careful thought and study to this question, the government has come to the conclusion that the existing legislation is not adequate. In particular it has been borne in upon us that there are a large number of returned men who, while not suffering from any disability immediately traceable to some particular happening, are nevertheless finding themselves breaking down through causes more or less unknown. In other words, they are experiencing after a number of years what I think would be described in medical terms as the effects of deferred reaction. Though they went through the strain of the war, though they suffered mentally and physically as they did in those years, the fact that at the time they were strong and in good health led to nothing being immediately visible as a consequence of the strain they had been called upon to endure. As the years have gone by however, and the system has weakened from other causes, the strain of past years has begun to tell and many men are breaking down today apparently for no other reason than that of the strain of the war period.
That is the opinion of a man who was for a long time the leader of the government of this country, and I believe he did give that question a lot of study. A great deal of study has also been given the same question by many others, but I think a little more help would be better than continued study. Are we withholding this help because we cannot afford it? I do not think so. At the present time our bins are full of grain. We are wondering how in the world we are going to get rid of it all; yet these veterans, who as I said before went over to defend Canada, are not getting the assistance to which they are properly entitled. Only the other day, and since the session commenced, we had the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) tell us that they were going to provide additional subsidies for gold mines. It would be much more appropriate if some of this assistance were made available so that our veterans could get better treatment.
There is another group of people I have been speaking about for the past few years, and thinking about in fact for much longer than that but holding back to some extent because of the survey that has been going on for the past number of years. I refer to the incapacitated. Each time we asked about them we were told that a survey was under way. I believe the survey is finished in most provinces at the present time, and I should like to know what action is now going to be taken. We know that many people who are in the very best of health are having difficulties, in some instances, through no fault of their own, in making a living. Then when we go about the streets and go into the homes and find people in wheel chairs or in bed and not able to take care of themselves we wonder why the country cannot


do something about it, particularly when the relatives, the parents, perhaps the brothers and sisters of these people are not able to help them without suffering themselves. When that pension is brought in, as I hope it will be during this session, I should like to see it enacted without a means test.
In connection with the people about whom I spoke a few moments ago, namely the veterans, while the legislation brought in at the last session did help to some extent, one change was made that I believe is not in keeping with our ability to provide further help. These people, single and married, cannot have outside earnings of more than $120 a year or $10 a month without having their war veterans allowance cut down. That is very poor business. While we have had a lot to say about health insurance at the present time, I think that giving these people an opportunity to get out and do a little work, if they are in physical shape to do it, would be one method of helping them attain better health. So, increase the allowable earnings.
I was glad to hear the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) announce the other day that the cattle embargo to the United States will be lifted on March 1. I am sure that will be welcome news to many of the cattle producers; and not only to them, because what is good for them is also good for the rest of the country. I hope that some suitable arrangements can be made so that those who have held cattle off the market will not lose on account of that embargo, and that full use will be made of the floor prices for beef until this problem has been brought down to normal again.
Many of our cattlemen have suffered much in dollars and in worry through no fault of their own and through no fault of the government, as far as foot-and-mouth disease is concerned. We blame them for a lot of other things, but they are not to blame for that particular calamity.
In connection with the question of pork I, like many others, was sorry to learn that the price will be down to 23 cents a pound after January 1. Today we have many people producing hogs, and when they find that the price at which they can sell is uneconomical they will naturally go out of business. Perhaps the result will be that some of those people who are protesting against the payment of subsidies or floor prices will find that because of the lower production of pork they will have to pay a much higher price because pork will not be produced. I know that at the present time we have plenty of pork to supply our market; but I am not satisfied that our market should be confined to Canada.

Only a couple of months ago I noticed that a considerable portion of it had been taken over by Denmark, something I was sorry to see. According to a newspaper item it appears that Great Britain has agreed to take at least 90 per cent of the exports from that country, and at substantial prices. More recently I noticed that Holland had made a short-term agreement along similar lines.
I believe that if some of our trade restrictions were removed, particularly those affecting our currencies, we would have kept much of that market, and the condition would be improved for people in other countries as well. I believe the government is making some attempt to remove some of the restrictions. We know the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) are in London at the present time. The stand they should take was made abundantly clear in the house before they left. They went to London with good intentions and, had they been able in a Liberal party of around 180 members to find another man able to assume the duties of deputy prime minister, perhaps our good friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) would have gone along, too. He seems to be the dealer in the family; and while he does not always make the best deals, the fact remains that he does make them.
A recent issue of the Ottawa Citizen indicates that the Minister of Trade and Commerce was in New York recently and spoke to the United States foreign trade council. The newspaper article contains some comment on his trip. He told them that-
-trade barriers have multipled in some countries at an alarming rate. But there are signs that countries with import controls now are more receptive to the idea of getting rid of them.
"How general that attitude has become, I do not know," said Mr. Howe, "but it has been in evidence in some very important quarters and it is certainly a most significant and welcome sign."
Some of the sterling area countries were trying to learn the precise and true causes of its dollar shortage, but, said Mr. Howe, the free world could not afford to postpone reduction of restrictions until this was done.
I am glad the Minister of Trade and Commerce is catching on to some of the things that are wrong.
Import restrictions, imposed for temporary purposes, had a way of becoming permanent. Quantitative controls on imports, imposed to halt a drain on dollar exchange, made a permanent cure for the dollar problem more difficult. The responsibility for removing the controls rested with countries which had imposed them. But he doubted whether they would be removed "without the encouragement and co-operation of our two countries and particularly the United States."
The time was ripe for a new attack on the world's trade restrictions, said Mr. Howe. He was confident that a world in which non-restrictive trade policies predominated could be re-established. But there
The Address-Mr. Fair was one "great essential"-a need for "close and tenacious co-operation by all the free nations-a resolute will to work together."
I hope the Minister of Trade and Commerce and his colleagues will work together to bring about the condition this article indicates. I believe the Canadian farmers could produce much more, both for the benefit of themselves and the country as a whole, and to relieve starving nations overseas. The farmers feel, however, that if they do not have some assurance of a market there is not much use in producing grain and livestock. Our experience in the past has been that unless we have some contracts, some method of getting rid of our products after they are produced, the farmer must take the rap in the form of lower prices. Certainly he derives no benefit from lower prices, because such prices do not apply to the same extent in respect of the articles he must use in order to produce.
Trade restrictions should be removed. I was glad to hear the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) early in this session, and on another occasion last session, set out some of the things that are happening in respect of prices in this country as compared with those in the country immediately south of us. Many of us who travel through the United States on our way to the west have purchased goods of different kinds in that country. Many times we are able to get them at no more than half the price we must pay on this side of the border.
We have the raw material in this country, and I do not think we are paying as high wages as are paid in the United States. Yet, because of the protection in different forms given to our manufacturers, our consumers are compelled on many occasions to pay 150 per cent of the amount that should be paid. As examples one thinks immediately of automobiles, tires, shoes, clothing and many other commodities. Especially is this true of electrical goods.
I was pleased to note that a little less than a year ago the government did introduce a bill to remedy this condition. While that legislation kept us here in Ottawa almost until Christmas day, and made it necessary to resume after Christmas, the bill was passed, and I believe it had much to do with cutting down the prices of goods. People are receiving as much as $150 trade-in allowance for some item of little value from the kitchen when purchasing a refrigerator, a stove, a washing machine or something of that nature.
For a few moments I should like to discuss the wheat situation. Before doing so, however, personally and on behalf of the people I represent I should like to compliment

The Address-Mr. Fair the chief commissioner and his associates in the Canadian wheat board. While they are continuously being sniped at by the Winnipeg grain exchange and their friends, it is my belief that the men in the wheat board have done a first-class job. The final payments announced a short time ago have made many of our farmers happy. In its restricted form the wheat board has done an excellent job; and when the Minister of Trade and Commerce makes his next trip to Washington I hope he will not permit himself to be tied down to the prices to which we have been subjected in the past.
The crops in 1950 and 1951 were two of the most difficult to handle. Despite out-of-condition and low-grade grain, the wheat board has done a job satisfactory to all, so far as I am aware. I hope they will continue in office and to do good work, even though some may wish to get rid of them. They are the farmers' salvation.
I should like now to discuss the international wheat agreement. In common with other hon. members who have already spoken, I would like to have a new one. I am not convinced that the terms of the present agreement are satisfactory or in the interests of our producers. The price ceiling is $1.80 per bushel in United States funds. For some months this gave the farmers an advantage whereby they received $1.98 per bushel for their top-grade grain, basis Fort William-Port Arthur-Vancouver. But, because of the fiddling around with our dollar and gold and other things connected with the monetary system, we find that at one time our Canadian dollar was at a premium of 5 per cent over the United States dollar. As a result there have been quotations for wheat under the international wheat agreement as low as $1.72 a bushel instead of the price of $1.98. This means a drop of 26 cents per bushel, and those on the sidelines do not see any reason whatever for that difference in price. When the present international wheat agreement was being negotiated we did not vote against it. We thought an international agreement was a good thing but, as I stated before, we were not satisfied with the terms. When we have a definite ceiling price on the grain that we are to sell over the four-year period without having any ceiling whatever on the costs of production, then I think we are stepping into very dangerous territory.
That was pointed out very clearly to the government by those in this group, and the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) made a suggestion one day that there should be a fluctuating price for our grain. In other words the price of our grain should be tied


to the price of goods in the importing countries, and if the price of goods in those countries went up then the price of our wheat would go up. If the price of goods in the importing countries went down then the price of wheat should go down correspondingly. By that method we would have the opportunity to bring back the same quantity of the other fellow's goods regardless of high or low price.
But the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) did not feel that it was possible to get figures upon which to base a deal of that kind. The hon. member for Acadia of course came back and told him that the international monetary fund had all these figures available and had had them for months past. But even with that information in the possession of the minister nothing whatever was done. As a result of the set-up hundreds of millions of bushels of wheat have been sold under the agreement at as much as 50 cents a bushel below the price of class II wheat, which is the wheat sold by the wheat board to countries other than those covered by the international wheat agreement.
I hope this pitfall will be avoided when the next international wheat agreement is negotiated. I understand the meeting is to be held in Washington on January 12, although some press reports state that an attempt is being made to delay the conference until after the new president takes office on January 20. We shall be quite satisfied to wait until after that date provided we can get a deal that is worth while. As I stated before, I should like the Minister of Trade and Commerce to go there in the same spirit evidenced in statements he has made during past weeks, when he has said that we are not going to be too easily satisfied. I believe an international wheat agreement is a good thing, but we must not sacrifice price and other things for the sake of getting such an agreement. The wheat board is doing a good job, and if we cannot get satisfactory terms under such an agreement then I believe the wheat board is also capable of doing this job.
Another matter that has been giving many people a lot of trouble is the question of supplying wheat to Canadian millers for consumption within Canada at the international wheat agreement price. That is a definite steal from the wheat growers of Canada because they get nothing whatever, not a single solitary cent, in return for that. On one occasion the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that he would not agree to the Canadian taxpayer subsidizing the wheat growers in order that the class II price might be paid them. There is no subsidy whatever connected with the matter and the people who

grow wheat and who take a reduced price, sometimes to the extent of 50 cents a bushel, are well aware of that fact. That is a part of the program.
In order to bring down the cost of producing wheat to some extent I would suggest, as I have on two or three other occasions, that an investigation be made into the cost of farm implements. We have examples of prices for farm machinery that are entirely unjustifiable. Cars and trucks are also used in connection with the production of grain, and I would suggest that something be done to find out why the prices of such items are so high compared with prices across the line. That is one way that we might help our producers to cut down the cost of production.
In order to make things better for our national safety, I would again urge the government to take into consideration the early construction of a highway from Winnipeg to the coast over the Yellowhead pass route. There is provision made for a highway in the southern part of western Canada, but Canada is a big country and its defence seems to be one of our worst headaches. We are contributing more than $2 billion a year toward the preparations. I think some of that money could well be spent in the building of a highway from Winnipeg through Saskatoon, my own home town of Vermilion, Edmonton, and on through the Yellowhead pass to Vancouver.
There is another item that has been talked about quite a lot, and on a few occasions I have mentioned it myself. I refer to taxation. We feel we have far too many taxes, far more than are necessary for the purposes for which they are levied. On this occasion, however, I want to deal with the problem of a particular case of taxation involving a farmer and his wife. Last session on July 4, the day we adjourned, I took up this matter, and before that I wrote the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) about it. I had very nice letters from him. He was most courteous, but I believe that somebody in his department is making wrong decisions because I know that the minister would not be guilty of making the decision which was made in the particular case with which I am going to deal for the next five minutes or so.
This case concerns a man and his wife. I believe they were married away back in 1914. At that time the wife would be about 20 and, as far as I can figure it out, her husband would be about 29. I remember that I got married once too, and I was about the same age as this man and my wife was about the same age as the lady involved. I can remember the enthusiasm with which we entered
The Address-Mr. Fair into the farming experience. In the particular case to which I am referring the lady concerned, either by using her own earnings or perhaps as a gift from her folks, was in possession of one cow and one heifer when she was married. They struggled along. They were living in a semi-dry part of the country, and even farmers living in the best part of the country have had quite a struggle all through the years from that time until now.
As I said, in 1914 this lady on her own account had one cow and one heifer. That makes two animals. In 1915, because it takes only nine months for an increase of one calf, there would be four head of cattle. In 1916 there would be six head in the ordinary course of events, and in 1917, provided some of the first calves turned out to be heifers, there would be an even greater increase. Anybody who wishes to do a little arithmetic may work out the problem for themselves. Of course there would have to be a lot of supposition because all calves are not heifers; some of them are bulls. I am bringing out the point at this time to show the nonsense that is sometimes practised in the Department of National Revenue. From 1914 to 1948 is a period of 34 years. With the natural increase of two calves a year, with only two cows being in the production line, we would have a total of 68 head of cattle. I will leave it at that for the time being.
As I stated before, plenty of lean years were experienced because this was a dry district. This lady and her husband worked hard, very hard. I do not know of any group of women in Canada who work as hard and for as long hours as do our farm women. That was particularly true in days gone by. As a result of her start of a herd of cattle she finally built up a nice herd and was able to purchase a half section of land. As time went on they, like a good many other people on the farm, had broken health. In 1948 they sold a part of their basic herd. I say "their" basic herd because I presume this man had some cattle of his own and the two herds grew up together, and naturally they carried on as they should have done. This lady believes there should be a community interest in the case of man and wife.
After selling a part of their basic herd they decided, for the security of the wife, that they would buy an annuity for her. They decided to buy a government annuity, ten years, guaranteeing $100 monthly. That annuity cost them $13,268.76. Looking at it from my point of view I believe the price was a little higher than it should have been. I have not inquired into that as it just caught my eye yesterday.

The Address-Mr. Fair
In 1948 the woman had $1,000 in her bank account and the husband apparently wrote the cheque which paid for the annuity, $13,268.76. The balance of the amount which accrued from sales of livestock, grain, et cetera, was in the husband's name. Over that account the wife had power of attorney. The husband, as I say, wrote the cheque to pay for the annuity for his wife and it must be clearly pointed out that the money they had in the bank and which was used to pay for that annuity was income from their farm operations and livestock. It had been fully assessed and full taxes had been paid to the Department of National Revenue. There is no argument so far. In my opinion the money belonged to them and they could do with it just as they saw fit.
When the annuity was purchased they were advised by the Edmonton office that there would be no tax since the purchase was made from income on which income tax had already been paid. They were advised that there might be tax on the interest portion of the annuity as they received it. In 1951 the husband was assessed gift tax of $1,184.63. That was protested immediately to the Department of National Revenue and an attempt was made to have the annuity cancelled. Of course that did not succeed, because if you buy a government annuity, I understand the money is there and you cannot do anything about it. You wait until it begins to pay and you carry on from there.
This all means that an annuity guaranteeing $100 a month for ten years cost them $13,268.76 plus gift tax of $1,184.63, or a total of $14,453.39. That was the family's own money. Had the wife written a cheque herself on her own account, if she had had $13,000 or $14,000 instead of $1,000, there would have been no attempt made to collect gift tax on the amount.
Should this lady, who is not now in good health, die after ten years she will have collected ten times $1,200 or $12,000. Without saying one word about interest it has already cost them $14,453.39. I believe quite sincerely that this gift tax was wrongly levied, as the wife's profits were lumped together with those of her husband. I point out that this team worked together on their farm. They worked hard, very hard. I know the territory in which they lived, and they had to work hard. In spite of that, because the man wrote the cheque he is assessed this amount of gift tax.
The wife had $1,000 in her own bank account, and I come back again to the herd of cattle that was started back in 1914 with two potential producers, one cow and one heifer. It is estimated by the Department of
IMr. Fair.]

National Revenue, I believe the Edmonton branch, that the $1,000 she had in the bank would account for the value of the two head of cattle she started with and any increase that should have accrued in the meantime. I think it is time that whoever did that figuring was sent out to a farm to get a little experience on the end of a fork handle or something else.
As I pointed out, from the two head she started with, in the 34 years between 1914 and 1948 there would have been a total herd of 68 head of cattle with only two producing each year. We should also remember that during recent years cattle were a fairly good price. One thousand dollars or -even fourteen thousand dollars would not begin to pay for the cattle that would have accumulated on this lady's own property plus the half section of land they purchased.
They protested to the department and could not get anything done. In my opinion, if the clerks in the Department of National Revenue office in Edmonton, and perhaps other centres as well, cannot figure dollars of assessment any better than they figured the offspring of those two head of cattle from 1914 on, then it is time something radical was done. There is an injustice here which the minister investigated after I took the question up last July. He wrote me a very nice letter. Again I say I am not accusing the minister of any of the injustice that has occurred in this case. I have known the minister here since 1935 and I would not for a moment think of attributing anything like that to him; but he is the minister responsible and he must take full responsibility for what is done by his officials in Edmonton and elsewhere.
I notice that the regulation is to the effect that overpayment of tax may be refunded to the taxpayer upon written application therefor if the request is received within twelve months of the overpayment. I am quite satisfied from what I have read that other farmers have found themselves in exactly the same position, and I am bringing the matter to the attention of the house for a second time so this injustice may be rectified. It is the minister's responsibility. This lady's husband, and the lady herself, have been wrongfully cheated out of $1,184.63 an,d I think it should be taken care of. I know the minister does not want to impose a wrong like that on a Canadian farmer or on anybody else. I believe I have placed their case fairly on the record today. I would ask the minister, in the name of justice, that consideration be given to this case. I understand that these people are now off the farm and are not working it any more. In the interest

of a little harmony and fair play in the country, I would ask the minister to investigate this case and make a refund of the amount I have mentioned. I hope the minister will do that because I know he does not want to be unfair. I have every confidence in him, and I hope this matter will be adjusted.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
In the
few minutes I have at my disposal before six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to one or two matters that concern my constituency more directly. First of all may I extend my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Deslieres) and seconder (Mr. Schneider) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne on the manner in which they both performed their tasks in the house. I should like to add one more word of congratulation to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) upon the very high position to which he has been named in the United Nations. As one who had the privilege and honour of serving under him at the fourth session of the general assembly I fully appreciate the task that he has been given as president of the general assembly. This is a tribute not only to him personally; it is certainly an indication of the high regard in which he is held at the United Nations, as well as a tribute to our country. I am very pleased to be able to extend my congratulations to him.
I want to refer briefly to the P.F.R.A. This afternoon mention has been made of the South Saskatchewan river project. I fully support this project and hope it will come to realization. At the same time, however, I should like to say that the magnitude of this important project that is being undertaken by the P.F.R.A. should not overshadow or relegate to the background the true purpose for which this splendid act was initiated. In the first place, all the people in the west know that this act has done a tremendous amount of good through the small, individual projects which have been carried out. We in the Red river valley are aware of this as well.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the Red river is known to be very temperamental. A few years ago we were complaining about having far too much water in our district, and this year the opposite is the case. The Red river is very low. Actually there is some fear that if this winter proves to be severe the river
The Address-Mr. Jutras might freeze solidly to the bottom, and the water may not be usable at all. However, we are used to that and we have many dug-outs which were built under P.F.R.A. Many farmers have more than one of these dugouts to assure a supply of water. This year, because of the dry season, most of these dug-outs are almost dry, and we may have a severe shortage of water during the winter.
I believe that the P.F.R.A. could help us, not so much financially but by helping us try to make greater use of the water we have at the present time. As a matter of fact, most of the farmers went to great expense this fall to get pumping equipment and hose by means of which they hoped to pump all the water available in the area into one dugout. On an individual basis this proved a rather costly operation. Possibly the P.F.R.A. could give consideration to renting whatever pumping equipment or hose they have so we could make use of every drop of water that is available in the area.
I want to say a word, too, about the Canadian farm loan board. They have been doing a very good job out west. There is an area in the southeast corner of Manitoba in which I think the Canadian farm loan board could do a great deal more than it has done in the past. I am sure the result of this increased activity would be almost to transform that southeastern corner of the province. The people in that area have been relying almost exclusively on pulpwood to earn their living. The supply is getting shorter all the time, and a great deal of that land is almost ready to be broken up and turned into agricultural production. I prophesy that in a few years you will see grain elevators there, and this will be very productive and high-priced land.
However, at the present time the farmers living there are short of cash. Since these farms have not been developed, the farmers have difficulty in getting credit and that is where I think the farm loan board could be of assistance. By a liberal use of credit this whole section of Manitoba could be transformed into a new and very productive source of foodstuffs for the years to come.
I should like to move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
